entities.name: Epigonus of Pergamum
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Epigonus of Pergamum stands as the preeminent court sculptor to the Attalid dynasty in Pergamum during the late third century BCE, a period of profound artistic innovation and political consolidation in the Hellenistic world. Operating under the patronage of Attalus I Soter (reigned 269–197 BCE), Epigonus became a central figure in the development of the Pergamene School of sculpture, renowned for its dramatic realism, intense emotional expression, and masterful portrayal of human suffering and heroism. His work profoundly shaped the aesthetic sensibilities of the Hellenistic age and left an indelible mark on subsequent Roman art.

The core of Epigonus's documented output, though largely known through Roman copies, consists of monumental commissions celebrating Attalid military triumphs, particularly the victories over the Galatians (Gauls) in Anatolia around 241 BCE. While no original signed works survive, ancient authors like Pliny the Elder attribute to him iconic pieces such as the "Dying Gaul" (often identified as the trumpet-player, a Gallic chieftain) and the "Gaul Killing Himself and His Wife," both part of large sculptural groups originally placed in the Sanctuary of Athena Nikephoros at Pergamum and later on the Acropolis in Athens. These sculptures captivated viewers with their meticulous anatomical detail, psychological depth, and a revolutionary approach to depicting non-Greek subjects with dignity and pathos, rather than mere caricature.
